characters: Kwame: a thoughtful eleven-year-old Ghanaian boy in Primary 6 in the fictional village of Nsuom, wearing a khaki school uniform and carrying a notebook.
Esi: Kwame’s eleven-year-old classmate and friend, wearing a khaki dress uniform and braided hair with blue beads.
Engr. Asante: a licensed hydrogeologist and water engineer with the Community Water and Sanitation Agency (CWSA), wearing a blue field shirt, hard hat and carrying geophysical survey instruments.
Nana Ofori: the respected village chief and chair of the Nsuom Water and Sanitation Management Team, wearing a traditional kente-trimmed cloth.

narrationPlan.voice: Warm, respectful Ghanaian English storyteller; wise, unifying tone for Nana Ofori and clear scientific authority for Engr. Asante.
narrationPlan.pace: Steady Upper Primary / JHS pace (~120 words per minute).
notes: Pronounce Kwame as KWAH-meh, Esi as EH-see, and Ofori as oh-FOH-ree.

culturalNotes: Affirms faith in God as a source of unity, gratitude and service while respecting Ghana’s religious diversity and upholding strict scientific standards for safe water.
reviewQuestions: Does the story clearly warn that a classroom sand filter does NOT remove pathogens or chemicals?
Are all community budget numbers (200 × 15 × 12 = 36,000 + 64,000 = 100,000 cedis) consistent throughout?

pages.brief: Sunny dry-season morning in a Ghanaian village: adults queuing patiently with yellow water containers near a padlocked broken hand-pump while Kwame (11, khaki uniform, notebook) and Esi (11, khaki uniform, blue beads) watch from the school path.
pages.narration: Empathetic, realistic opening showing the community impact of a broken water system.

pages.brief: Warm community gathering under a large baobab tree in Ghana: Nana Ofori in traditional cloth, seated alongside respected male and female elders from Christian, Muslim and traditional backgrounds, speaking calmly to attentive villagers.
pages.narration: Respectful, inclusive tone showing unity across diverse faiths.

pages.brief: Close view at the durbar: villagers smiling and nodding in unity as Nana Ofori gestures toward a notebook and a map of the village held by the Water and Sanitation Management Team.
pages.narration: Warm, dignified delivery affirming that faith inspires diligence, science and service.

pages.brief: Ghanian Primary 6 science classroom: teacher holding a demonstration plastic bottle layered with pebbles, sand and cloth over a jar of water, holding up a warning hand while Kwame and Esi take notes.
pages.narration: Emphasise strongly that a simple classroom sand/cloth filter does NOT make water safe to drink.

pages.brief: Science classroom chart (visual icons only, no text): large brown dirt particles trapped by sand grains at the top, while tiny glowing green microbe icons pass through into the bottom cup unless professionally treated and lab-tested.
pages.narration: Crystal-clear scientific safety distinction between sediment filtration and pathogen/chemical removal.

pages.brief: Grassy hillock outside the village: Engr. Asante (blue CWSA shirt, white hard hat) reading a portable digital geophysical resistivity meter connected to ground stakes, explaining an underground rock-layer diagram to Nana Ofori, Kwame and Esi.
pages.narration: Exciting scientific discovery explaining aquifers and hydrogeology.

pages.brief: Community meeting table: Engr. Asante pointing to a colour-coded site blueprint showing a solar borehole on a green hillock well separated from lower village buildings, with Kwame and Esi observing.
pages.narration: Explain safe borehole siting and the 100,000-cedi project cost clearly.

pages.brief: Village community centre veranda: the female treasurer, Nana Ofori, Kwame and Esi standing beside a large public ledger board with neat bar columns and receipt books (no readable text).
pages.narration: Read the community budget math step by step: 200 × 15 = 3,000 cedis/month; × 12 = 36,000 cedis; + 64,000 grant = 100,000 cedis.

pages.brief: Sunny hillside outside Nsuom: professional water technicians installing solar panels and a raised black water storage tank over a clean concrete-sealed borehole pad while villagers watch safely from a fenced path.
pages.narration: Emphasise financial transparency, community compassion and sanitary engineering.

pages.brief: At the new standpipe: Engr. Asante wearing nitrile gloves filling a sterile glass sample bottle from the tap, and holding a green-stamped laboratory certificate beside Nana Ofori (no readable text).
pages.narration: Crucial safety lesson: clear groundwater must still pass accredited laboratory testing for microbes and chemicals before anyone drinks it.

pages.brief: Joyful sunny scene in Nsuom: clear water pouring from a tiled four-tap standpipe into clean buckets while local technicians in tool belts check the solar array on the tank tower behind them and Kwame and Esi celebrate.
pages.narration: Joyful celebration of sustainable maintenance and community success.

pages.brief: Bright schoolyard morning: Kwame and Esi washing their hands with soap at a clean school tap fed by the village solar water tank, smiling warmly.

teacherGuide.overview: A Primary 5 to JHS 1 science, civic-leadership and values story set in the fictional village of Nsuom. Learners see how faith in God inspires unity, diligence and service alongside scientific hydrogeology, strict water-safety rules (why classroom filters never make water drinkable), laboratory testing, transparent public budgeting and preventive maintenance.
learningGoals: Explain why a simple sand-and-cloth filter only removes visible sediment and NEVER removes microscopic pathogens or dissolved chemicals.
Describe how groundwater is stored in underground aquifers and why boreholes must be sited uphill from latrines, sealed and laboratory-tested.
Calculate multi-step community project budgets (200 households × 15 cedis × 12 months = 36,000 cedis + 64,000 grant = 100,000 cedis).
Explain how faith-inspired values, interfaith unity, scientific expertise and transparent public accounting work together to solve community problems.

beforeReading: Ask learners: "If a glass of water looks crystal clear, does that guarantee it is safe to drink? Why or why not?"
Emphasise that in Ghana’s communities, people of different faiths live and work together in mutual respect.
whileReading: Pause at page 5 to stress the safety rule: NEVER drink water from a classroom sand filter or untreated stream.
Pause at page 8 to verify the community contribution arithmetic on the board.
afterReading: Have learners design a simple "Preventive Maintenance Schedule" for a school asset (such as a Veronica bucket stand, school borehole, library books or classroom desks).
discussion: Why did Nana Ofori and the religious leaders say that waiting passively without planning or working is not true stewardship?
Why did Engineer Asante refuse to let anyone drink the clear borehole water until the laboratory certificate arrived?
Why did the old hand-pump stay broken for six months, and how did the new 500-cedi monthly maintenance fund prevent that mistake from happening again?
reflection: What Would You Build, Discover or Change? What shared facility in your school or neighbourhood needs better care or a maintenance plan, and how can students contribute safely?

mathsExtension.task: Nsuom puts 500 cedis per month into a bank maintenance account. After 24 months (2 years), how much has been saved, and if a replacement solar pump controller costs 4,200 cedis, how much remains in the maintenance fund after paying for the repair?
mathsExtension.answer: Saved in 24 months: 500 × 24 = 12,000 cedis. Remaining after repair: 12,000 − 4,200 = 7,800 cedis.

mathsExtension.task: In the 100,000-cedi borehole project, the grant covered 64,000 cedis and the community raised 36,000 cedis. What percentage of the total cost did the community raise?

support: Draw the underground cross-section showing rain soaking into soil → porous rock aquifer → sealed borehole pipe → storage tank → tap.
stretch: Research the roles of the Community Water and Sanitation Agency (CWSA) and the Ghana Standards Authority (GSA) in setting safe drinking-water standards (GS 175).

culturalNotes: In Ghanaian towns and villages, Water and Sanitation Management Teams (WSMTs) work with traditional authorities, Assembly Members and diverse religious communities to manage rural water systems.
localiseThis: Discuss where your school’s drinking and handwashing water comes from (GWCL pipe, CWSA borehole, sachet water, rainwater harvesting) and how it is kept safe.

whatWeKnow: Simple mechanical filtration through gravel, sand and cloth removes suspended turbidity (sediment) but does NOT remove dissolved chemicals or microscopic pathogens (bacteria, viruses, protozoa).

Safe rural drinking-water engineering requires hydrogeological siting, sanitary borehole sealing, accredited laboratory testing (microbiological and physicochemical under GSA GS 175 / WHO guidelines) and residual disinfection.
Dedicated community maintenance funds and trained local technicians dramatically reduce rural borehole downtime.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Hydrogeologists in Ghana use satellite remote sensing and geophysical mapping to chart deep Basement Complex fracture aquifers resilient to multi-year droughts.

investigation.title: See Why Sediment Filtration Is Only Step One (Non-Drinkable Demo)
materials: A clear plastic bottle with the bottom cut off by the teacher
Clean pebbles, coarse sand, fine sand and a piece of clean cotton cloth
A jar of muddy water mixed with a drop of safe food colouring (to represent dissolved substances)
steps: Have the teacher secure the cloth over the bottle neck and layer pebbles, coarse sand and fine sand inside to model how soil layers trap large dirt particles.
Pour the muddy coloured water through the sand layers into a clear cup below.
Observe that while the brown mud particles are trapped by the sand, the food colouring (and any invisible microbes) passes right through into the cup!
investigation.whatToNotice: The coloured water in the bottom cup proves that even when big mud particles are filtered out, dissolved substances and microscopic germs pass straight through, which is why classroom-filtered water must NEVER be drunk!
investigation.safetyNote: STRICT SAFETY RULE: Label the cup "DO NOT DRINK, SCIENCE DEMO ONLY" and pour the water on outdoor plants after the demonstration; wash hands with soap and safe running water.

factCheck.claim: A simple sand-and-cloth filter removes suspended sediment but does not make water microbiologically or chemically safe to drink.
factCheck.explanation: Pore spaces in simple sand and cloth filters (typically >10–50 micrometres) are far larger than bacteria (~0.5–5 micrometres), viruses (~0.02–0.3 micrometres) and dissolved ions (fluoride, arsenic, nitrates), requiring disinfection and laboratory verification.
factCheck.reference: World Health Organization (WHO) Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality; Ghana Standards Authority GS 175.

pronunciation.guidance: "KWAH-meh". English speakers often say "KWAH-mee"; confirm the final vowel.
reviewerNotes: Confirm final vowel (meh vs mee) and the "kw" onset.
